sections.section_title: Authority Over Sin Demonstrated Through Healing
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage escalates Jesus's demonstrated authority to the domain of sin itself, with the healing of a paralytic serving as visible proof that 'the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,' provoking the scribes' charge of blasphemy and the crowds' fearful glorifying of God.

sections.section_title: The Calling of a Tax Collector and Table Fellowship with Sinners
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage presents Jesus calling Matthew from the tax booth and eating with tax collectors and sinners, defining his mission through the physician metaphor and citing Hosea 6:6, and stating 'I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.'

sections.section_title: The Question About Fasting and Three Analogies
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage explains why Jesus's disciples do not fast through three analogies -- the bridegroom's presence, unshrunk cloth on an old garment, and new wine in old wineskins -- all pointing to the qualitative newness of the present moment that cannot be contained in old forms.

sections.section_title: A Ruler's Daughter and a Woman with Chronic Bleeding
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage presents two interwoven healing accounts -- a ruler's dead daughter raised and a woman with a twelve-year hemorrhage healed -- both involving faith expressed physically and conditions of ritual impurity, demonstrating that Jesus's authority overrides contamination by sending wholeness in the opposite direction.

sections.section_title: Two Blind Men: The Son of David and the Demand for Faith
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage presents the first public use of the title 'Son of David' for Jesus, with healing granted 'according to your faith,' reinforcing the pattern that faith -- active trust expressed in concrete action -- is the operative condition for receiving what Jesus offers.

sections.section_title: The Mute Demoniac and Two Competing Interpretations
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage juxtaposes two opposite responses to the same evidence: the crowds marvel that 'never was anything like this seen in Israel,' while the Pharisees attribute Jesus's power to 'the prince of demons,' crystallizing the structural division between crowds and leaders that will deepen throughout the document.

sections.section_title: Sheep Without a Shepherd and the Need for Laborers
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds this passage closes the section with a summary nearly identical to 4:23, presents Jesus's visceral compassion for crowds who are 'harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd,' evoking Ezekiel 34's indictment of Israel's failed leaders and God's promise to shepherd through David's heir, and transitions to the commissioning of the twelve through the image of a plentiful harvest needing laborers.
